Immunosuppressants have been tried in the treatment of multiple sclerosis (p.892), al- though in some studies the benefit obtained may have been outweighed by toxicity. Myasthenia gravis. Patients with myasthenia gravis (p.629) who require immunosuppression are usually treat- ed with corticosteroids. Azathioprine is used mainly in myasthenia gravis for its corticosteroid-sparing effect but may also be of use when corticosteroids are contra-indicat- ed or when response to their use alone is insufficient. Ciclosporin, mycophenolate mofetil, and tacrolimus have been tried similarly. Ocular disorders Immunosuppressants have been used with some success in ocular disorders with inflammatory or immunological components. In scleritis and uveitis (see p.1512 and p.1515) corticosteroids, given topically, intra-ocularly, or systemically are widely used when treatment is needed, but in unresponsive disease, or in patients with unaccepta- ble adverse effects, immunosuppressants such as azathio- prine, ciclosporin, or mycophenolate mofetil, may be giv- en. Daclizumab, leflunomide, sirolimus, and tacrolimus have also been tried in uveitis. Immunosuppressants may be valuable in the management of Behçet’s disease, rheu- matoid arthritis, or Wegener’s granulomatosis, (see p.1499, p.11, and p.1515, respectively), including their as- sociated ocular lesions. Ciclosporin or azathioprine have been used with corticosteroids in the management of both ocular and vascular symptoms of Cogan’s syndrome (p.1502). Ciclosporin has also been used topically in cor- neal ulceration, see p.1831. In Graves’ ophthalmopathy (see under Hyperthyroidism, p.2165), ciclosporin with oral glucocorticoids has been used as an effective alternative treatment. Reviews. 1. McCluskey PJ, et al.
